narrative.summary_main:
- **Your portfolio's job** — Your portfolio is meant to fund retirement at 65 and your children's college costs, all from one salary. Today it sits almost entirely in taxable and cash accounts, with nothing in retirement accounts. The projection shows savings running out at age 73, and that is your main gap.

- **What the numbers say** — Guaranteed income covers 25% of your $153,672 yearly retirement spending need. Your average yearly draw would be 12.2% of savings at the start of retirement. Your strengths are real: $80,000 in cash covering 7.9 months of essentials, no debt, and a 24% savings rate.

- **Directions to consider** — Protection is now in place, with $2,000,000 of term life inside the recommended $1,250,000 to $2,500,000, a $2,000,000 umbrella that meets the minimum, and long-term disability cover. So the studies point first to retirement saving: you could contribute up to $4,400 to an HSA and up to $7,500 to a deductible traditional IRA, with nothing contributed to either today. Then comes the $98,838 college need, with Ethan's $12,500 payment due August 2027.

- **One caveat** — We don't know whether an employer 401(k) is available to you, so we draw no conclusion there. Cost basis and purchase dates are missing for your taxable holdings, which limits tax-lot analysis. Roth IRA contributions are not permitted for you.

- **Worth watching** — Cash above your reserve and near-term goals is only $750 after $18,500 of goals. After expenses and savings you are about $6,418 a year short. Technology is 30.6% of your stock holdings. None of this is urgent, but keep an eye on it.
narrative.snapshot_main: This snapshot draws on the accounts you hold: a brokerage account of about $300,000, two custodial accounts for Ethan and Ava of about $35,000 combined, and $80,000 of cash in checking and savings. All of it is held by you, as the only adult in the household. Taken together, your investments lean heavily toward stocks, held mostly through broad US funds.
narrative.portfolio_today_intro: This portfolio leans toward stock growth, yet it has to carry several jobs at once: income in retirement, two college starts, and a near-term cash need, all drawing on the same limited pool of savings. Growth-oriented investing, concentrated in one market and one sector, brings larger swings in value, while some of what the household must fund falls due within a few years and cannot easily wait out a downturn. The evaluation that follows looks at how well the portfolio's present behavior fits those competing jobs for you and your two children.
narrative.portfolio_today_what_it_needs_to_do:
- **Retirement income** — You plan to retire at 65, and guaranteed income covers about 25% of what you expect to spend. The projection shows savings and investments running out at age 73, so this money has to help close that gap over the long term. Your retirement accounts hold nothing today, so your brokerage account, cash and guaranteed income carry this job.
- **College for Ethan and Ava** — Ava starts in August 2028, and Ethan's next payment of $12,500 is due August 2027. About $98,838 is still needed beyond current college-account balances, which are $0. Part of this money has a short timeline, and it competes with retirement for the same savings.
- **Near-term cash** — Your $80,000 of cash covers about 7.9 months of essential expenses, or 6.1 months after the vacation in January 2027 and Ethan's college payment. Those goals total $18,500. That leaves only about $750 above your reserve, so this money has to stay available and steady, especially while your yearly cash flow runs about $6,418 short.
- **Children's custodial money** — The two custodial accounts hold about $35,000 combined and are held for Ethan and Ava. Their job is to serve the children, separate from your own retirement and cash needs.
narrative.portfolio_today_what_its_actually_doing:
- **Stock-heavy growth** — Your long-term accounts are 84.6% stocks against an 80.0% target, and the children's accounts are almost entirely stocks. That gives strong growth potential and bigger swings in value. Over three years the mix returned 15.6% a year, in line with a comparable diversified portfolio. Money needed for college within a few years rides the same swings.

- **One sector, one market** — Technology is 30.6% of your stock holdings and 92.6% is in the United States, above the 85% line. Both come from the funds you own, since you hold no individual stocks. In practice, your results lean heavily on one sector and one country. Your $250,000 salary is also 17.9% of your net worth.

- **Tax cost in taxable accounts** — Every investment dollar sits in taxable accounts, which lose about $3,032 a year to tax. Dividends taxed at 35.8% drive most of it. JNK costs $1,229 and SCHD in your brokerage account costs $853. Because 93.0% of the bill sits in the brokerage account, that account sets most of your yearly drag.

- **No retirement balances** — Your retirement accounts hold nothing, so retirement depends on the brokerage account, your cash and guaranteed income. Your $80,000 of cash covers 7.9 months of essentials, but only $750 sits above the reserve and near-term goals. With a $6,418 yearly shortfall, that cushion is thin if goals recur.
narrative.portfolio_today_performance_timeline:
Over the three years from November 2023 to November 2026, your portfolio grew an average of 15.56% a year. A diversified portfolio holding the same overall share of stocks grew 16.97% a year, so you trailed it by about 1.4 percentage points. Against the Growth benchmark set at your target mix, which returned 17.62%, the shortfall was about $2,270 over the period. That is a small gap, and the paths stayed close. Your value swung less than the comparison (8.88% against 10.30%). Your return for each unit of risk taken was 1.35 against 1.30. Your worst fall was 11.95%, against 13.35% for the comparison, and it was recovered in 78 days.

The most meaningful pattern is how you moved in rising and falling markets. You captured about 66% of the market's gains and about 90% of its losses. So you gave up more of the upside than you saved on the downside. Your three long-term investment accounts, about $335,000 together, returned about 19.4% a year. That was slightly ahead of their own comparison on return for each unit of risk (1.43 against 1.40). Three years is a short history, so treat these readings as a description of the period, not a forecast.

Two moments in the data show the cushioning. In the April 2025 tariff-pause rally, you fell 2.52% against 3.78% for the comparison. After the Federal Reserve's final rate hike in July 2023, you fell 4.60% against 5.60%. Both differences are modest and come from a short record, so they show a tendency and do not prove one.
narrative.portfolio_today_whats_working:
- **Cash reserve** — You hold $80,000 in checking and savings, covering 7.9 months of essential expenses, or 6.1 months after your January 2027 vacation and Ethan's August 2027 college payment. You carry no debt, so an income disruption would not force you to sell investments in a downturn.

- **Saving habit** — You save $60,000 a year, which is 24% of your $250,000 gross pay and above the 20% benchmark we look for. Money moves into investments every year as a set habit, not from whatever remains at year-end.

- **Simple, low-cost structure** — You hold eight positions in broad, low-cost ETFs, such as VTI at a 0.03% expense ratio, and no individual stocks. No single company can sink the portfolio, and none of your funds duplicate each other within the same category.

- **Resilience in market stress** — Your portfolio returned 15.6% annualized over three years with 8.9% volatility and a Sharpe ratio of 1.35, against 1.30 for a comparable diversified portfolio. In the April 2025 tariff pause you fell 2.52% against 3.78%, and in the July 2023 Fed final hike 4.60% against 5.60%.

- **Money set aside for the children** — Your two custodial accounts hold about $35,000 combined in VTI and SCHD: $20,000 for Ethan and $15,000 for Ava. They returned about 21.7% and 21.9% annualized over three years, showing you have funded the children's future steadily.
narrative.portfolio_today_priorities:
- **Retirement shortfall** — Your projection shows savings and investments running out at age 73, with an average draw of 12.2% at the start of retirement and $0 in retirement accounts. This is the largest planning gap, so the portfolio needs a clearer, deliberate role in funding retirement income.

- **Yearly shortfall** — After expenses of $129,600, which now include the new insurance premiums, your savings capacity is a shortfall of $6,418 a year. You are saving while running a small negative balance, so the cash cushion of about $750 will not refill from cashflow.

- **College funding** — About $98,838 is still needed for college, and your 529 balance is $0. Ethan's $12,500 payment is due in August 2027. This competes with retirement while you run a $6,418 yearly shortfall, so how existing savings are directed matters most.
narrative.portfolio_today_verdict: You hold no retirement accounts today, so the balances are 0, but what you are doing right is saving steadily: your 24% savings rate ($60,000 a year) is strong, and because it sits in cash and taxable accounts it stays accessible. The vulnerability is that nothing is building in a retirement account, so your projection shows savings and investments running out at age 73, with $1,448,673 of planned spending unpaid by the end of the plan at age 91. Guaranteed income of $38,336 a year covers 25% of the $153,672 yearly spending need, which leaves a $115,335 annual gap and an average draw of 12.2% of savings at the start of retirement. You have 17 years until your target retirement age of 65, so there is still time to change this, but college costs for Ethan and Ava will compete for your savings, which now run a yearly shortfall of $6,418 after the new insurance premiums. You could contribute up to $7,500 to a deductible traditional IRA, with 0 contributed so far, while Roth IRA contributions are not permitted for you; the employer-plan limit is $24,500, but whether you have a 401(k) is not in the data, so no conclusion can be drawn there. The next step is a clear, sequenced path for retirement saving, set against the college timeline, that redirects part of what you already save rather than adding to it.
narrative.portfolio_today_also_meaningful: You have no HSA today: nothing has been contributed, and you could contribute up to $4,400 a year if your health plan is HSA-eligible. At your 32% rate, that would save about $1,408 in tax each year, a concrete return for a small change. Your yearly cashflow is currently about $6,418 short, so treat this as a secondary step. Retirement funding, where your savings run out at age 73, and closing that shortfall come first. An HSA contribution fits after those, and you can size it to what your cashflow allows, for example by redirecting part of the $60,000 you already save each year instead of adding new money. Eligibility and your health plan are not in the data yet, so confirm that your plan qualifies before you contribute. The tax-drag review shows no HSA-related cost, so the case rests on the tax savings from contributing.
narrative.recommendations_main:
- **Protect the children first** — Your $2,000,000 of term life insurance sits within the recommended range of $1,250,000 to $2,500,000, and long-term disability cover is in place. With two dependents, this protects Ethan and Ava if your income stopped. Keeping this cover in place as they head to college is worthwhile.
- **Close the umbrella and property gap** — Your $2,000,000 umbrella policy meets the recommended minimum, so there is no umbrella gap. Your home and the Porsche Cayenne still show as uninsured. Because your assets are substantial, one liability claim could reach your savings, so confirming cover on both is worthwhile.
- **Start building retirement savings** — Your retirement account balances are $0, and the projection shows savings running out at age 73. Retirement is 17 years away, so steady contributions can still change this. The sooner this is addressed, the more it can help you provide for the years ahead.
- **Use tax-advantaged accounts if they are open to you** — If your health plan qualifies, you could contribute up to $4,400 to an HSA, with $0 contributed so far. That is worth about $1,408 a year in tax at 32%. Whether you have a workplace 401(k) is unknown, so we draw no conclusion there. After expenses and savings you are about $6,418 a year short, so redirecting what you already save, rather than adding more, keeps this realistic.
- **Plan for college within your cash** — College funding still needed is $98,838, and Ethan's $12,500 payment is due August 2027. Your $80,000 of cash is strong, but only $750 sits above your reserve and near-term goals. With a yearly shortfall of $6,418 rather than a surplus, savings will not refill that cushion, and college and retirement saving compete for money that is not there yet.
- **Keep an eye on concentration and tax cost** — Technology is 30.6% of your stock holdings and US exposure is 92.6%. Your investments also cost about $3,032 a year in tax, with JNK the largest piece at $1,229. Broadening exposure and easing that tax cost would make your portfolio more resilient. Cost basis and purchase dates are missing, so adding them would help.
narrative.recommendations_scenarios:
- **Calmer than a comparable portfolio in three of the sharpest pullbacks** — In the 90-day tariff pause episode (April 2025), your portfolio fell 2.52% while a diversified portfolio with the same overall stock share fell 3.78%. When the Fed ended its rate hikes (July 2023), you fell 4.60% against 5.60%. When the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs (February 2026), you fell 0.96% against 1.68%. In each case you lost less than the comparison: 1.26, 1.00 and 0.72 percentage points less. These are past results and do not promise the same in future.
- **A fair picture, including the weak spot** — In the Liberation Day tariff drop (April 2025), you fell 9.87% against 9.51%, slightly more than the comparison. That was your largest single-event fall. Over the full three years the portfolio's worst peak-to-trough fall was 11.95%, milder than the 13.35% for the comparison portfolio, and it recovered in 78 days.
- **Smoother ride, with a trade-off** — Your portfolio earned 15.56% a year over three years, against 16.97% for the comparison. It moved less, with volatility of 8.88% against 10.30%. It kept about 66% of the market's gains in rising periods and took about 90% of its losses in falling ones. So it gave up more of the upside than it saved on the downside. Return per unit of risk was 1.35 against 1.30, so overall efficiency is in line.

rules: These facts are the only figures to quote for these concepts. Quote the label's meaning with the number; never relabel a fact as another one.
Each fact names the facts it must not be confused with. Never call one by the other's name.
Keep the unit: a USD/yr figure is always said per year, a lump sum never is.
Do not add, subtract or compare two facts unless a fact says how they relate.
Never quote a date that is before the plan date.
Write a date as month and year (August 2039), never as an ISO date (2039-08-01).
Write a ratio or rate as a percentage (55%), never as a decimal (0.551).

A fact's `replaces` lists key-metric fields that hold the same or a confusable figure under a misleading name. When you see one of those fields in your other inputs, quote the fact with its label instead. Field names are never labels.

events.description: The Fed raised rates 25bp to 5.25–5.50%, the 11th and final hike in the cycle — the highest level in 22 years. The Fed held here for 14 months before cutting in September 2024.
events.name: Fed final hike to 5.25–5.50%

events.description: Fed held rates steady but the dot plot signaled 75bp of cuts in 2024, marking a decisive pivot. S&P 500 surged to new highs; Russell 2000 +4%. Long-end yields fell sharply. Catalyzed a broad year-end rally across equities and bonds.
events.name: Fed pivot — December 2023 dot plot

events.description: Yen carry trade unwind and US recession fears triggered a global rout. Japan's TOPIX fell 12.3% — worst since 1987 Black Monday. VIX spiked above 65 intraday. S&P 500 fell ~3% at the open but recovered most losses by Friday. The episode lasted one week.
events.name: Global selloff — VIX spikes above 60

events.description: First Fed rate cut in four years, and an outsized 50bp move, formally marking the start of the easing cycle. Signaled the Fed's confidence that inflation was heading sustainably toward 2% and opened the door to subsequent cuts.
events.name: Fed first rate cut — 50bp

events.description: Trump defeated Kamala Harris decisively. S&P 500 surged 2.5%, Dow +3.6%, Russell 2000 +5.8%. The "Trump trade" lifted banks, small caps, and crypto on expectations of deregulation and tax cuts. USD strengthened sharply.
events.name: Trump election win

events.description: Chinese startup DeepSeek released an open-source AI model rivaling GPT-4 at a fraction of the cost, questioning the US AI capex thesis. Nvidia lost $589B in market value — the largest single-day loss for any stock in history. Nasdaq fell 3.1%, S&P 500 fell 1.5%.
events.name: DeepSeek AI shock

events.description: Trump announced sweeping reciprocal tariffs (10% baseline, 34% on China, 20% on EU, 46% on Vietnam) — the highest US tariff level since 1909. S&P 500 lost 10% in two days — the worst two-day loss in history ($6.6T erased). Long-end yields spiked on bond vigilante concerns.
events.name: Liberation Day tariffs announced

events.description: After the S&P 500 fell 10% in two days post-Liberation Day, Trump announced a 90-day pause on reciprocal tariffs above 10% for all countries except China (raised to 125%). S&P 500 surged 9.52% — its largest single-day gain since 2008. Nasdaq jumped 12.16%. Record 30B shares traded.
events.name: 90-day tariff pause rally

events.description: After two days of talks in Geneva, the US and China agreed to reduce reciprocal tariffs from 125% to 10% for 90 days. S&P 500 surged 3.3%, Nasdaq +4.4%. Apple and Amazon led gains as the deal eased supply-chain fears for import-dependent tech and retail sectors.
events.name: US-China Geneva tariff truce

events.description: The Supreme Court affirmed that the Trump administration's use of emergency powers to impose the April 2025 reciprocal tariffs was unlawful, formally unwinding the tariff regime's legal basis. (Exact date to verify on next run.)
events.name: Supreme Court strikes down Liberation Day tariffs

events.description: US and Israel launched coordinated airstrikes on Iranian military and nuclear sites, with nearly 900 strikes in the first 12 hours. Iranian leadership was decapitated. Brent crude surged 10–13% immediately; global equity markets sold off sharply on escalation and energy-supply fears.
events.name: Operation Epic Fury — US-Israel strikes on Iran

periods.character: Fed held rates at 5.25–5.50% for 14 months while inflation ground lower. US equities (led by Mag-7/AI) still delivered strong returns despite restrictive policy.
periods.name: Higher-for-longer plateau
periods.portfolioExperience: Mixed-to-positive: short-duration cash delivered attractive carry, US large-cap led by AI themes, long-duration bonds struggled.

periods.character: After 10Y yield peaked at 5% on Oct 19, cooling inflation data and the Fed's December dot-plot pivot catalyzed a powerful simultaneous rally in equities and bonds through year-end.
periods.name: Q4 2023 rate-pivot rally
periods.portfolioExperience: Strongly positive: both equity and fixed income rallied, rewarding duration and risk after a painful Q3.

periods.character: Three consecutive cuts (-50bp, -25bp, -25bp) took the policy rate from 5.25–5.50% to 4.25–4.50%, supporting risk assets even as the December cut was delivered in a hawkish package.
periods.name: Fed easing cycle — initial phase
periods.portfolioExperience: Positive: equities and duration both rallied through the fall before the December hawkish cut capped the move.

periods.character: Trump's decisive election victory sparked a rally in domestic-focused assets — small caps, banks, crypto, defense — on expectations of deregulation and tax cuts. S&P 500 hit all-time high Feb 19.
periods.name: Post-election "Trump trade"
periods.portfolioExperience: Positive for US-tilted portfolios, especially small-cap and value; international allocations lagged as USD strengthened.

periods.character: Escalating tariff threats against Canada, Mexico, and China — compounded by DeepSeek's AI disruption — reversed the post-election rally. S&P 500 fell 10% from its February all-time high.
periods.name: Pre-Liberation Day correction
periods.portfolioExperience: Moderately negative: US large cap led losses; international equities held up better as the "US exceptionalism" trade unwound.

periods.character: Liberation Day tariffs triggered the worst two-day S&P loss in history ($6.6T erased); the 90-day pause the following week triggered the largest single-day gain since 2008. Geneva truce and S&P ATH by June 27 closed the episode.
periods.name: Tariff shock & recovery
periods.portfolioExperience: Negative turning strongly positive: V-shaped recovery rewarded investors who stayed allocated; international equities outperformed the full year.

periods.character: Repricing away from the 2025 "soft landing + AI boom" narrative toward sticky core inflation, Middle East conflict premium in oil, elevated long-end Treasury yields, and US large-cap underperformance vs. international.
periods.name: Sticky-inflation / geopolitical risk regime
periods.portfolioExperience: Mildly negative: US large-cap drawdown cushioned by international equity, short duration, and energy exposure.
